story: In Norse mythology, two tribes of gods, the Æsir and the Vanir, had fought a long war. To seal peace between them, both sides spat into a vat. Not wanting the truce-symbol to go to waste, the gods shaped the spittle into a man named Kvasir. He was extremely wise, able to answer any question put to him, and he traveled far and wide teaching mankind and spreading knowledge. Eventually two dwarfs, Fjalar and Galar, invited Kvasir to their home for a private talk. When he arrived, they killed him and drained his blood into two vats, called Són and Boðn, and a pot called Óðrerir. They mixed the blood with honey to create the Mead of Poetry, a drink that would make whoever tasted it a poet or scholar. When the Æsir asked after Kvasir, the dwarfs lied, saying he had suffocated from his own intelligence, since no one was learned enough to question him. The mead eventually passed through the hands of the god Odin and came to mankind, bringing them the gift of poetry. Kvasir also played a role in catching the trickster god Loki, who had turned into a salmon to hide from the gods after causing the death of the god Baldr. When the gods reached Loki's hideout, Kvasir was the first to enter, and being the wisest of all, he recognized the shape of a fishing net in the ashes of a fire. He told the gods, who used the pattern to fashion a net and capture Loki from a river, binding him afterward as punishment.
